You are a mentor in a study hub. Answer in English, briefly and to the point.

Topic: How an LLM works (grade G0)

Goal: Understand that an LLM scores the next token at every step, and how this relates to training and the transformer.

Done criteria:
1. Explain that at each step the model outputs probabilities for the next token and text is produced by a loop: pick a token, append it to the input.
2. Tell training (weights change, expensive) from inference (weights fixed, token-by-token generation).
3. Describe at diagram level that tokens become vectors and attention layers relate tokens to each other.

Materials:
- How do Transformers work? (Hugging Face LLM Course, ch.1): https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter1/4
- The Illustrated GPT-2 (Jay Alammar): https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-gpt2/
- Transformer Explainer (Georgia Tech, poloclub): https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/
- nanochat: the best ChatGPT that $100 can buy (Andrej Karpathy, GitHub): https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat
- Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., arXiv 1706.03762): https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

Task: Explain this topic in plain words: what it is, why an engineer who works with AI agents needs it, and how to check that I understood it. Give 3 self-check questions.

response.text:
# How an LLM works (G0)

## What it is

**1. Next-token prediction in a loop.**
An LLM is a function: it takes a sequence of tokens (pieces of words) and returns a **probability distribution over the whole vocabulary** for the *next* token. That's all one step produces.

Text is generated by a loop:

```
tokens = tokenize(prompt)
repeat:
    probs = model(tokens)          # e.g. "Paris": 0.92, "Lyon": 0.03, ...
    next  = pick(probs)            # greedy, or sample with temperature/top-p
    tokens.append(next)
until next == <end> or max_tokens reached
```

The model has no plan for the whole answer. Each token is chosen given everything before it, including tokens the model just produced itself.

**2. Training vs inference.**

| | Training | Inference |
|---|---|---|
| Weights | **Change**, nudged so the correct next token gets higher probability | **Fixed** |
| Data | Trillions of tokens, plus fine-tuning/RLHF for chat behaviour | Your prompt |
| Cost | Huge (GPU-months, $$$), done rarely | Cheap per call, done constantly |
| Output | A new set of weights | Text, one token at a time |

When you chat with a model it does **not learn** from you. Anything it "remembers" is either in its weights from training or in the current context window.

**3. Transformer, at diagram level.**

```
tokens → embeddings (vectors) + position info
       → [ attention → feed-forward ] × N layers
       → final vector → probabilities over vocabulary
```

- Each token becomes a **vector**, a list of numbers that encodes its meaning.
- **Attention** lets each token look at earlier tokens and pull in information from the relevant ones. For example, in "The cat sat because **it** was tired", `it` attends to `cat`.
- Stacking many layers builds richer, context-aware representations.
- The last position's vector is turned into next-token probabilities.

## Why an agent engineer needs this

- **Context is the only memory.** An agent "knows" only what is in the weights plus what you put in the prompt. Tool results, history and instructions all compete for the context window.
- **Hallucinations make sense.** The model outputs a *plausible* next token, not a verified fact. That's why you need grounding, tool calls and validation.
- **Sampling settings matter.** Temperature/top-p change `pick()`. Low means more deterministic, high means more varied. The same prompt can give different outputs.
- **Cost and latency scale with tokens.** Input is processed once, but output comes out token by token. Long outputs are slow, and long contexts are expensive.
- **Tool calls are just tokens too.** The model emits text in a tool-call format, and your harness parses and executes it. Malformed output is always possible.
- **"Teaching" an agent means prompting/context, not training**, unless you actually fine-tune.

## How to check you understood

You understood it if you can, without notes:
- draw the generation loop and say where the probabilities come from;
- say which of training/inference changes weights and why chatting doesn't;
- sketch tokens → vectors → attention layers → probabilities and say what attention does in one sentence.

Hands-on: open **Transformer Explainer**, type a prompt and watch the probability bar for the next token change as you move temperature.

## 3 self-check questions

1. A model writes a 50-token answer. How many forward passes (loop iterations) produce it, and what exactly does each pass output?
2. Yesterday you corrected an agent's mistake in chat. Today, in a new session, it makes the same mistake. Explain why in terms of training vs inference, and name two ways to fix it.
3. In "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because **it** was too big", which mechanism lets the model link `it` to the right noun, and what is it operating on: words, or something else?

Send me your answers and I'll check them.
